Geometry is the branch of mathematics concerned with the properties, relationships, and measurements of points, lines, planes, and solid shapes. Emerging from practical surveying needs in ancient civilizations, it developed into an abstract logical system that became the foundation of mathematical reasoning itself. Through the work of ancient Greek philosophers and mathematicians, geometry evolved from empirical observation into a formal discipline based on axioms and proofs, establishing a model of rigorous reasoning that influenced all subsequent mathematics and science.

The earliest geometric knowledge arose from practical necessity: ancient Egyptians needed to resurvey land after Nile floods, while Babylonians calculated areas and volumes for agriculture and construction, establishing geometry as grounded in the physical world. Greek mathematicians transformed geometry into an abstract, proof-based system. Euclid's Elements, written around 300 BCE, systematized geometric knowledge into definitions, postulates, and logical proofs, establishing the axiomatic method that became the model for all mathematics. Archimedes advanced geometric understanding through rigorous study of circles, spheres, and parabolas, and his method of exhaustion anticipated calculus by calculating areas and volumes through limiting processes.

The Platonic solids—the five regular polyhedra—captured ancient fascination with perfect geometric forms and symmetry. These shapes appear in nature, art, and philosophy as emblems of mathematical beauty and cosmic order. The Pythagorean theorem, relating the sides of right triangles, became perhaps mathematics' most famous result. Its discovery prompted the realization that some quantities—irrational numbers—could not be expressed as ratios, expanding mathematical understanding. Euclidean geometry remained unchallenged until the nineteenth century, when mathematicians discovered non-Euclidean geometries where parallel lines behave differently—a revolution in mathematical thinking with implications for physics and relativity.

Geometry's applications span architecture, engineering, astronomy, art, and navigation. Understanding geometric proportions, angles, and spatial relationships remains essential to designing structures, mapping celestial bodies, and representing three-dimensional space on two-dimensional surfaces. Modern geometry encompasses diverse subdisciplines including projective geometry, topology, differential geometry, and algebraic geometry, extending far beyond classical plane and solid geometry.
